properties.name: Vesuvius
properties.one_line: Vesuvius erupted without warning on August 24, 79 CE, burying Pompeii and Herculaneum under volcanic debris and killing thousands nearby. Pliny the Younger watched the ash column rise from across the Bay of Naples and later described his uncle's fatal rescue attempt in two famous letters. By 117 CE farmers had already returned to plant vines on its fertile lower slopes, unaware the mountain could erupt again. No one in the region had even considered it a volcano before that day.
properties.image_credit: Pierre-Jacques Volaire, 18th-century painting of an eruption of Vesuvius · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 18th-century painting of Vesuvius erupting at night over the Bay of Naples

properties.name: Etna
properties.one_line: Etna towered over eastern Sicily as the largest active volcano in the Mediterranean, its summit crater rarely without a plume of smoke. Ancient writers recorded a violent eruption in 122 BCE that buried nearby Catania under debris and ash. Greek and Roman myth chained the giant Typhon beneath its fires and placed Hephaestus's forge inside the mountain. Sailors used its glow as a nighttime landmark for approaching Sicily's eastern coast.
properties.image_credit: The eruption of Mount Etna, 17th-century etching, Wellcome Collection · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Historical etching showing Mount Etna erupting with lava flowing toward the coast

properties.name: Stromboli
properties.one_line: Stromboli erupted in small, steady bursts every twenty minutes or so, a rhythm so constant that sailors nicknamed it the lighthouse of the Mediterranean. Greek and Roman myth placed Aeolus, keeper of the winds, on this island, ruling his floating kingdom from its shores. Ships navigating between Italy and Sicily used the glowing summit to fix their position after dark. The volcano has erupted in essentially this same pattern for over two thousand years.
properties.image_credit: Stromboli erupting, Aeolian Islands · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Photograph of Stromboli volcano erupting with glowing lava against a dark sky

properties.name: Vulcano
properties.one_line: Vulcano gave its name to every volcano on Earth, since Romans believed its sulfurous crater sat directly above the forge of Vulcan, god of fire. Thick yellow fumes and boiling mud pools surrounded the main cone, convincing ancient sailors they had found the gods' own furnace. Aeolian islanders mined sulfur and alum straight from its flanks and traded them across the Roman world. The island's Latin name, Vulcania, later gave English the word volcano itself.
properties.image_credit: Aerial view of the La Fossa crater, Vulcano · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Aerial photograph of the sulfur-stained La Fossa crater on the island of Vulcano

properties.name: Mount Olympus
properties.one_line: Mount Olympus rose over 2,900 meters above the Thermaic Gulf, its jagged summit wrapped in cloud so often that Greeks and Romans placed the throne room of Zeus there. Homer described golden gates guarded by the Horae opening onto an eternal, storm-free peak reserved for the twelve Olympian gods. No ancient writer records anyone reaching the true summit, leaving the gods' exact home unconfirmed by human eyes. Farmers in its foothills watched snow cap the peak nearly year-round.
properties.image_credit: Mount Olympus seen from Litochoro, Greece · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Photograph of the snow-streaked peaks of Mount Olympus rising above forested foothills

properties.name: Mount Argaeus
properties.one_line: Argaeus rose to roughly 3,900 meters over the Cappadocian plain, its snow-streaked cone visible for miles across the region's volcanic landscape. The geographer Strabo wrote that no one in his lifetime had ever climbed all the way to its summit, and locals treated the peak as sacred ground. Cappadocian kings struck coins showing the mountain topped with a star, tying their dynasty's legitimacy to it. The provincial capital, Caesarea, took its skyline from Argaeus looming behind it.
properties.image_credit: Mount Erciyes, ancient Argaeus, Cappadocia, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Photograph of the snow-capped volcanic cone of Mount Argaeus over the Cappadocian plain

properties.name: Mount Zaphon
properties.one_line: Mount Zaphon rose only about 1,700 meters above the Syrian coast, yet Canaanite and Greek worshippers alike treated its summit as a divine throne, home to Baal-Hadad and later identified with Zeus Kasios. Ugaritic texts centuries older than Rome describe Baal's palace built there of silver and lapis lazuli. Hadrian would climb it within years of taking power in 117 CE to watch the sunrise from its altar. Ships approaching nearby Seleucia Pieria used its peak as a landfall marker.
properties.modern_location: Kel Dağı / Jebel al-Aqra, Hatay Province, Turkey
properties.image_credit: Jebel Aqra (Mount Kasios / Zaphon), Syria-Turkey border, 2008 · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Photograph of Mount Zaphon rising above the Syrian coastline

properties.name: Mount Ida
properties.one_line: Mount Ida rose above the Troad's coastal plain, its forested slopes supplying timber for the ships Homer's heroes launched against Troy. The Iliad staged the judgment of Paris here, where a Trojan shepherd prince awarded Aphrodite a golden apple and doomed his city to war. Priests of Cybele, the Great Mother, kept a cult center on its heights that Roman poets like Virgil traced back to Aeneas's flight from Troy. Springs on the mountain fed the rivers that watered the Troad below.
properties.image_credit: Summit shrine on Kaz Dağı, ancient Mount Ida of the Troad · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Photograph of a shrine near the summit of Mount Ida in the Troad, Turkey

properties.name: Mount Ida
properties.one_line: Mount Ida rose over 2,450 meters as Crete's highest peak, and a cave near its summit was venerated across the Greek world as the birthplace of Zeus. Priests said the infant god's cries were drowned out by clashing bronze shields so his father Cronus would not hear him. Pilgrims left bronze votive shields and figurines in the cave for centuries, many later recovered by archaeologists. Cretan coins stamped Zeus's cave onto their currency well into the Roman period.
properties.image_credit: Mount Ida (Psiloritis), Crete, seen beyond olive groves · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Photograph of Mount Ida on Crete rising behind terraced olive groves

properties.name: Mount Kithairon
properties.one_line: Mount Kithairon divided Boeotia from Attica, its slopes soaked in some of Greek tragedy's darkest myths. Herdsmen exposed the infant Oedipus here on his father's orders, and Euripides staged Pentheus's death at the hands of frenzied Bacchae on this same mountain. A biennial fire festival, the Daidala, once burned wooden effigies on its summit to honor Hera. Shepherds still grazed flocks across its slopes throughout the Roman period, indifferent to the mountain's grim reputation.
properties.image_credit: Mount Kithairon, Boeotia-Attica border, Greece · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Photograph of the ridgeline of Mount Kithairon between Boeotia and Attica

properties.name: Mount Helicon
properties.one_line: Mount Helicon held the sacred springs of Aganippe and Hippocrene, waters said to grant poetic inspiration to anyone who drank from them. Hesiod claimed the Muses appeared to him on its slopes and handed him a laurel staff while he tended sheep, launching Greek didactic poetry. A sanctuary of the Muses stood in the mountain's Valley of the Muses, drawing poets and pilgrims for centuries. Pausanias toured its shrines within decades of 117 CE and recorded statues still standing there.
properties.image_credit: Maerten van Heemskerck, "Concert of Apollo and the Muses on Mount Helicon," Chrysler Museum of Art · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 16th-century painting of Apollo and the Muses gathered on Mount Helicon

properties.name: Mount Parnassus
properties.one_line: Mount Parnassus rose more than 2,450 meters above Delphi, its twin peaks called the Phaedriades framing the oracle sanctuary at its base. Greeks and Romans alike considered it Apollo's mountain and the meeting place of the nine Muses, sacred ground distinct from the temple complex below. The Corycian Cave high on its slopes held centuries of votive offerings to Pan and local nymphs. Snow crowned its summit through much of the year, visible for miles across the Gulf of Corinth.
properties.image_credit: James Skene, 19th-century watercolor of Mount Parnassus near Daulis · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 19th-century watercolor depicting Mount Parnassus above the Greek countryside

properties.name: Delos
properties.one_line: Delos measured barely 5 square kilometers, yet Greek myth held that Leto gave birth to Apollo and Artemis here after Zeus anchored the once-floating island to the seabed. A sanctuary of temples, treasuries, and stone lions grew around the birth site over centuries. Rome declared the island a free port in 166 BCE, briefly making it one of the Mediterranean's busiest slave markets before pirates sacked it in 88 BCE. By 117 CE Delos survived mostly as a quiet pilgrimage ruin.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of the Temple of Apollo, Delos · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Photograph of the ruined Temple of Apollo on the island of Delos

properties.name: Samothrace
properties.one_line: Samothrace rose sharply from the northern Aegean to Mount Fengari, at nearly 1,611 meters the tallest peak in the Aegean Sea. Homer placed Poseidon on this very summit, watching the battle for Troy unfold across the water below. The island's height made it a landmark sailors used to navigate the open sea route between the Hellespont and mainland Greece. Its steep, harborless coastline kept Samothrace remote even as its famous sanctuary drew pilgrims from across the Mediterranean.
properties.image_credit: The island of Samothrace, northern Aegean Sea · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Photograph of the steep, mountainous coastline of Samothrace island

properties.name: Ortygia
properties.one_line: Ortygia formed the small island heart of Syracuse, joined to the mainland by a short causeway and centered on the freshwater spring of Arethusa. Greek myth told how the nymph Arethusa fled the river god Alpheus under the sea from Greece and resurfaced here as a spring, fresh water yards from the saltwater harbor. Ancient writers marveled that objects dropped into Greece's Alpheus River were said to reappear at this fountain. Papyrus plants, otherwise unknown in Europe, grew wild along its banks.
properties.image_credit: The Fountain of Arethusa with papyrus plants, Ortygia, Syracuse · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Photograph of the Fountain of Arethusa on Ortygia island, ringed with papyrus

properties.name: Scylla and Charybdis
properties.one_line: The Strait of Messina narrows to barely 3 kilometers between Italy and Sicily, its currents and whirlpools giving rise to a myth of two sea monsters devouring passing ships. Homer's Odyssey placed the six-headed Scylla on one rocky shore and the whirlpool Charybdis on the other, forcing Odysseus to choose the lesser evil. Roman sailors treated the crossing with caution, since tidal currents through the strait ran dangerously fast. The Calabrian town of Scilla still carries the monster's name.
properties.image_credit: Artistic depiction of Scylla and Charybdis in the Strait of Messina · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Artwork depicting the mythical sea monsters Scylla and Charybdis

properties.name: Cape Malea
properties.one_line: Cape Malea juts from the southeastern Peloponnese into open water, and ancient sailors dreaded rounding it more than almost any other point in the Mediterranean. Unpredictable winds and sudden storms off the cape wrecked so many ships that a Greek proverb urged sailors to forget their homes once they had passed it. Homer's Odyssey blew Odysseus badly off course here, delaying his return by years. Merchant ships often crossed the Corinth isthmus overland specifically to avoid this passage.
properties.image_credit: Cape Malea and Elafonissos island, NASA ISS photograph · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Satellite photograph of Cape Malea at the tip of the southeastern Peloponnese

properties.name: Pillars of Hercules
properties.one_line: The Pillars of Hercules marked the narrow strait between the Rock of Gibraltar and the North African coast, the westernmost edge of the world Greeks and Romans considered known. Myth held that Hercules split a single mountain in two, or dragged its peaks apart, to open a sea passage during his tenth labor. Beyond the pillars lay the Atlantic, called Oceanus, treated as the boundary of the habitable earth. The later motto non plus ultra, nothing further beyond, grew from this exact spot.
properties.image_credit: The Rock of Gibraltar, 1810 painting · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Early 19th-century painting of the Rock of Gibraltar overlooking the strait

properties.name: Fontes Sequanae
properties.one_line: The springs of Fontes Sequanae fed the source of the Seine River near Dijon, where Gauls and later Romans worshipped the healing goddess Sequana. Pilgrims threw more than a thousand wooden and bronze votive offerings into the sacred pool, many carved as eyes, limbs, and organs representing ailments they hoped the goddess would cure. A bronze statuette found at the site shows Sequana standing in a duck-prowed boat, arms spread in welcome. The spring still flows from the same plateau today.
properties.image_credit: Bronze statuette of the goddess Sequana in her duck-prowed boat, found at Fontes Sequanae · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Bronze figurine of the goddess Sequana standing in a duck-shaped boat

properties.name: Fontes Aponi
properties.one_line: Fontes Aponi supplied Padua's countryside with thermal water surging out of the ground at nearly 80 degrees Celsius, among the hottest natural springs Romans knew of. Worshippers credited the healing waters to the local god Aponus and built an oracular shrine here that used lots to answer visitors' questions. The poet Martial praised the springs' curative reputation in verse during the late 1st century. Wealthy Romans built villas near the site specifically to take the waters.
properties.image_credit: Entrance to the Montirone archaeological park, site of the Roman-era Fontes Aponi springs, Abano Terme · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Photograph of the entrance to the Montirone park at the site of ancient Fontes Aponi

properties.name: Fons Bandusiae
properties.one_line: Fons Bandusiae survives today only through the ode Horace addressed to it around 23 BCE, promising the spring a sacrificed kid goat for its cool water on the hottest days. Its exact location is disputed, with the strongest tradition pointing to a site near the poet's Sabine farm outside Licenza, east of Rome. Horace boasted the spring would grow more famous than any named in Greek poetry, a claim history validated. No inscription has confirmed which spring he meant, so the site stays unsettled.
properties.image_credit: The spring traditionally identified as Fons Bandusiae, near Licenza, Italy · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Photograph of a small spring in the Sabine hills traditionally identified as Fons Bandusiae

properties.name: Solfatara
properties.one_line: Solfatara formed a shallow volcanic crater near Pozzuoli, its cracked yellow floor venting sulfurous steam at temperatures near 160 degrees Celsius. Romans believed the site was the entrance to Vulcan's forge and named it the Forum Vulcani, ground that seemed to breathe fire underfoot. Bathhouses nearby channeled the crater's heat into steam treatments, popular with wealthy visitors to Baiae. Ancient visitors said walking the crater floor made a hollow sound, as if the ground beneath was empty.
properties.image_credit: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, drawing of the Solfatara at Pozzuoli, 1787 · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 18th-century drawing of the steaming sulfur crater of Solfatara near Pozzuoli

properties.name: Pamukkale
properties.one_line: Hierapolis grew around white travertine terraces, formed as hot springs cascaded down a cliff nearly 200 meters high, cooling into stepped pools of mineral stone. Romans built the city above a spring called the Sacred Pool, believing its waters healed alongside a lethal cave nearby, the Plutonium, sacred to Pluto. Ancient writers described birds dropping dead from vapors at its entrance, later traced to carbon dioxide gas. The terraces gave the site its modern name, cotton castle.
properties.image_credit: White travertine terrace pools at Pamukkale, near Hierapolis · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Photograph of white mineral travertine terraces and pools at Pamukkale

properties.name: The Siq at Petra
properties.one_line: The Siq formed a natural sandstone gorge over a kilometer long, cut by flash floods into walls that rise as high as 182 meters on either side. Nabataean engineers carved votive niches, water channels, and a dam into the rock to control flooding and guide pilgrims toward the city's facades. Walking the winding passage, visitors emerged at its far end facing Al-Khazneh, the Treasury, cut into the cliff face. Trajan had annexed the Nabataean kingdom as Roman Arabia just years before 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: The Siq, the narrow sandstone gorge leading into Petra, Jordan · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Photograph of the narrow sandstone gorge of the Siq leading into Petra

properties.name: Lake Fucino
properties.one_line: Lacus Fucinus filled a landlocked mountain basin with no river outlet, so it flooded nearby farmland every hard winter. Emperor Claudius spent years driving a tunnel through the surrounding hills to drain it, then marked the unfinished project in 52 CE with one of the largest mock naval battles Rome ever staged, throwing 19,000 condemned combatants onto warships on the lake itself. A mechanical silver Triton reportedly rose from the water to signal the start. The tunnel clogged and the lake barely dropped, defeating both Claudius and, later, Hadrian; it stayed a glittering, stubborn plain of water for centuries afterward.
properties.modern_location: Fucino plain, near Avezzano, Abruzzo, Italy
properties.image_credit: Fresco map of Lake Fucino, Gallery of Maps, Vatican Museums · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Historic fresco map showing Lake Fucino before its drainage

properties.name: Lake Trasimene
properties.one_line: Lake Trasimene's northern shore narrowed into a shelf of hills that Hannibal used to spring the deadliest ambush Rome ever walked into. On a foggy morning in 217 BCE his Carthaginian army fell on the marching column of consul Gaius Flaminius from three sides at once, pinning the Romans between the water and the slopes. Roughly 15,000 legionaries died in a few chaotic hours, some drowning in the shallows as they tried to flee, and the disaster forced Rome to appoint the dictator Fabius Maximus, whose delaying tactics later helped turn the war. Travelers in 117 CE still walked the same lakeside road past the killing ground.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of Lake Trasimeno from Castiglione del Lago · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: View across Lake Trasimene toward Castiglione del Lago

properties.name: Lake Avernus
properties.one_line: Lacus Avernus filled a volcanic crater so thick with sulfurous fumes that Romans believed no bird could fly over it, and its Greek-derived name meant roughly 'without birds.' Virgil sent his hero Aeneas down into the underworld through a cave beside its shore, cementing the lake's reputation as the gate of Hades itself. In 37 BCE Agrippa transformed this eerie, sacred water into a secret naval base for Octavian's war fleet, cutting a canal to the sea and boring a tunnel nearly one kilometer long through the hills to link it with Cumae. Warships now launched from what poets had called the mouth of the underworld.
properties.image_credit: Lake Avernus, oil painting by Richard Wilson (1713-1782) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 18th-century painting of Lake Avernus in its volcanic crater

properties.name: Lake Lucrinus
properties.one_line: Lacus Lucrinus was a shallow lagoon shut off from the Bay of Naples by a narrow causeway, and it produced the most celebrated oysters in the Roman world. Around 100 BCE the engineer Sergius Orata pioneered oyster farming there, tying young oysters to bundles of twigs so they could be lifted and moved at will, a technique that turned Lucrine oysters into a byword for luxury dining across the empire. The state leased its fisheries to contractors at steep prices, and villas belonging to men like Cicero lined its banks. Diners judged an oyster's quality simply by whether it had come from the Lucrine Lake.
properties.modern_location: near Pozzuoli and Baiae, Campania, Italy
properties.image_credit: Photograph of Lago di Lucrino, Campania · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: View of Lake Lucrino near the Bay of Naples

properties.name: Lake Bolsena
properties.one_line: Lake Bolsena filled the crater of an extinct volcano and remains the largest volcanic lake in Europe, its waters wide enough to hold two wooded islands near its center. Its shoreline city, Volsinii, was the wealthiest Etruscan settlement of its day until Rome sacked it in 264 BCE for allowing enslaved rebels to seize power, then deported the survivors and forced them to rebuild an entirely new town on the eastern shore. The refounded Roman Volsinii grew a forum, amphitheater, and baths within a few generations. By 117 CE it stood as a settled municipium beside a lake Romans simply called Lacus Volsiniensis.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of Lago di Bolsena · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: View across Lake Bolsena, the largest volcanic lake in Europe

properties.name: Lake Albano
properties.one_line: Lake Albano fills a volcanic caldera in the Alban Hills with no natural drain, and during Rome's long siege of Etruscan Veii its water level rose without explanation despite a drought. An oracle declared that Veii would fall only once the lake's waters were released, so Roman engineers cut an emissarium, a drainage tunnel more than a kilometer long, straight through solid volcanic rock to regulate the level. Veii fell soon after, in 396 BCE, and the tunnel still functions today. Latin peoples had already held the lake sacred long before Rome existed, and it remained a place of ritual reverence through the imperial period.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of Lake Albano and Monte Cavo · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Lake Albano seen with Monte Cavo rising behind it

properties.name: Lake Nemi
properties.one_line: Lake Nemi sits in a small crater tucked inside the outer ring of the Alban volcano, its still water so mirror-flat that Romans called it Speculum Dianae, the Mirror of Diana. On its northern shore stood one of Latium's richest sanctuaries, dedicated to Diana of the Wood, where worshippers whose prayers had been answered walked a torchlit procession around the entire lake wearing wreaths. The sanctuary's priest, the Rex Nemorensis, held his position only by killing his predecessor in single combat, a grim rite that persisted into the imperial era. Decades after 117 CE, Caligula would have enormous pleasure barges built to float on this same glassy water.
properties.image_credit: View of Lake Nemi, 1843, painting by Jules Coignet, National Gallery of Art · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 19th-century painting of Lake Nemi in its wooded crater

properties.name: Lake Como
properties.one_line: Lacus Larius, now Lake Como, stretched in a narrow Y-shape between steep Alpine slopes that Julius Caesar's forces secured in 49 BCE. The senator and writer Pliny the Younger, who grew up on its shores, owned two villas on the lake he nicknamed Comedy and Tragedy for their contrasting settings, one perched dramatically on a ridge and the other sitting right at the water's edge. He described the lake fondly in his letters, including an account of a mysterious spring nearby that rose and fell several times a day. Wealthy Romans kept building villas along its shores well into the second century CE.
properties.image_credit: Como and Lake Como, painting by Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 19th-century painting of Lake Como with the town in the foreground

properties.name: Lake Garda
properties.one_line: Lacus Benacus, the largest lake in Roman Italy, stretched more than 50 kilometers between the Alpine foothills and the Po plain. At its southern tip the poet Catullus owned a peninsula villa at Sirmio, which he called the jewel of every island and peninsula, writing of his sheer relief at being home again and sleeping in his own bed. A grand Roman villa later built on that same peninsula, popularly but mistakenly nicknamed the Grottoes of Catullus, became one of the largest private residences in northern Italy. Wealthy Romans lined the lake's shores with villas through the first and second centuries CE.
properties.image_credit: Panorama of Lake Garda · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Panoramic view across Lake Garda

properties.name: Lake Maggiore
properties.one_line: Lacus Verbanus, fed by the Alpine river Ticinus as it poured out of the mountains, linked Roman Italy to trade routes running north into Raetia. Ships crossed the lake and continued down the Ticino River to Pavia, then onward along the Po to the Adriatic, making it a working artery of commerce rather than just a beauty spot. Before Rome's arrival, the Iron Age Golasecca culture had already settled its shores for centuries, and Roman roads later threaded along the lake to move goods and legions toward the Alpine passes. By 117 CE it sat within the administrative orbit of Mediolanum, modern Milan.
properties.image_credit: Lake Maggiore in the Evening, painting by Ivan Aivazovsky (1892) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 19th-century painting of Lake Maggiore at dusk

properties.name: Lake Bracciano
properties.one_line: Lacus Sabatinus filled a volcanic caldera just northwest of Rome and, by the early second century CE, had become one of the capital's lifelines. In 109 CE Emperor Trajan opened the Aqua Traiana, an aqueduct that gathered fresh spring water from the hills around the lake and carried it many kilometers to power watermills and fill baths on Rome's Janiculum Hill. The lake itself stayed largely untouched, its springs simply tapped at the source, so it kept its wooded volcanic shoreline while feeding one of the newest aqueducts serving the capital during Trajan's reign, right around the time this map is set.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of Lake Bracciano · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: View across Lake Bracciano, source of the Aqua Traiana

properties.name: Lake Geneva
properties.one_line: Lacus Lemannus marked the edge of the known Roman world when Julius Caesar first campaigned in Gaul, its shoreline forming a natural wall against tribes to the north. In 58 BCE, worried that the migrating Helvetii would cross Roman territory, Caesar destroyed the bridge at Geneva and built a rampart and ditch nearly 30 kilometers long, running from the lake to the Jura mountains, to block their path. The tactic worked, forcing the Helvetii to seek another route and drawing Caesar into the wider war that conquered Gaul. By 117 CE Roman villas and vineyards lined its long crescent shore.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of Lac Léman (Lake Geneva) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: View across Lake Geneva toward the Alps

properties.name: Lake Constance
properties.one_line: Lacus Brigantinus took its Roman name from the tribal town of Brigantium on its northeastern shore, in the province of Raetia. In 15 BCE the future emperors Tiberius and Drusus led a Roman fleet onto the lake to crush Celtic resistance in one of the closing battles of Augustus's conquest of the Alps, a naval engagement fought at a lake few outsiders had previously known existed. Roman geographers such as Pliny the Elder recorded its waters afterward, and roads soon linked Brigantium into the network binding the Alpine provinces to Italy. By 117 CE the lake anchored a settled Roman frontier along its shores.
properties.image_credit: Satellite image of Lake Constance (Bodensee) · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Satellite view of Lake Constance on the Alpine frontier

properties.name: Lake Copais
properties.one_line: Lake Copais spread across the Boeotian plain as a shallow, marshy expanse so famous for its eels that the comic playwright Aristophanes joked about them onstage in Athens more than once. Bronze Age engineers had already dug canals and dykes to drain parts of the basin over a thousand years earlier, one of the most ambitious hydraulic projects of the ancient Aegean. By the Roman period the lake still flooded and shrank with the seasons, and the traveler Pausanias, writing not long after 117 CE, described its fish and reed beds among the finest in Greece. Local fishermen and eel-sellers remained a fixture of Boeotian life throughout antiquity.
properties.image_credit: Kopaissee (Lake Copais), 1839 painting by Carl Rottmann · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 19th-century painting of the Boeotian plain and Lake Copais

properties.name: Lake Karla
properties.one_line: Lake Boibeis spread across a low basin in Thessaly beneath Mount Pelion, a body of water old enough to appear in Homer's Iliad among the Thessalian contingents bound for Troy. Ancient poets and geographers, including Pindar, mentioned its shores and the town of Boebe beside it, and local myth held that the god Apollo had once been married there. The lake swelled and shrank unpredictably with mountain streams that had no clear outlet, flooding nearby farmland without warning. By 117 CE it lay within the Roman province of Achaea, a modest but storied lake whose name outlived most of the towns around it.
properties.image_credit: Lake Karla, Thessaly, Greece · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: Lake Karla in Thessaly

properties.name: Lake Stymphalia
properties.one_line: Lake Stymphalia filled a closed mountain basin in Arcadia with no river outlet, its water draining instead through underground sinkholes, a landscape strange enough to seed one of Greece's darkest myths. Ancient storytellers held that man-eating birds with bronze beaks and metal feathers nested in its marshes until Heracles drove them off with a rattle forged by the god Hephaestus, completing his sixth labor. The traveler Pausanias later described the lake and a shrine to Stymphalian Artemis on its shore during his journeys through Arcadia. The lake's unpredictable, sink-and-swell behavior kept it a source of local legend well into the Roman period.
properties.image_credit: Hercules at Lake Stymphalos, painting by Gustave Moreau · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: 19th-century painting of Heracles fighting the Stymphalian birds

properties.name: Lake Moeris
properties.one_line: Lake Moeris filled the Faiyum depression west of the Nile, an enormous natural reservoir that pharaonic engineers had already linked to the river by canal nearly two thousand years before Rome ruled Egypt. Around 1800 BCE, Pharaoh Amenemhat III built dikes and sluices to control its water precisely, using the lake to absorb Nile flood surges and irrigate the surrounding depression even in low-flood years. Roman administrators inherited this system largely intact after annexing Egypt in 30 BCE and kept the Faiyum among the empire's most productive grain-growing regions. The historian Herodotus, writing centuries earlier, had marveled that the lake seemed too vast and well-ordered to be entirely natural.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of Lake Moeris (Birket Qarun), Faiyum · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: View of Lake Moeris in the Faiyum depression

properties.name: Lake Mareotis
properties.one_line: Lake Mareotis lay just south of Alexandria, linked to the Nile's Canopic branch by canal and to the city's own harbor by another channel, making it the quieter, freshwater counterpart to the Mediterranean at the city's front door. Vineyards and olive groves covered its shores, and Mareotic wine, a pale, mild white, was exported across the Mediterranean in amphorae produced by a thriving local pottery industry. Grain barges and passenger boats crossed the lake constantly, since traffic from the Nile Valley reached Alexandria more easily by water than overland. By 117 CE the lake's harbors handled a large share of the goods flowing into one of the empire's greatest cities.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of Lake Mariout (Mareotis) near Alexandria · Wikimedia Commons
properties.image_alt: View of Lake Mareotis south of Alexandria

properties.name: Sea of Galilee
properties.one_line: The Sea of Galilee filled a freshwater basin below sea level in northern Judaea, ringed by nine or ten thriving towns whose wharves formed an almost unbroken line around its shore. Roughly 230 fishing boats worked its waters at the height of the Roman period, and the catch was salted and exported across the empire from a town whose Greek name, Tarichaea, literally meant 'salted-fish town.' Herod Antipas founded Tiberias on its western shore and named it for the reigning emperor, and by 117 CE the lake and its fisheries anchored the region's economy and daily life alike.

properties.name: Dead Sea
properties.one_line: The Dead Sea, called Lacus Asphaltites by Roman writers, sat so heavy with salt and minerals that nothing could sink in it and no fish could survive its water. Chunks of natural bitumen periodically floated to the surface, and locals paddled out in boats to haul the material ashore, cut it into blocks, and sell it across the eastern Mediterranean for uses ranging from shipbuilding to embalming. The historian Josephus and the geographer Strabo both described the strange lake and its floating asphalt trade in detail. Nabataean traders and Judaean rulers fought over control of this resource for generations before Rome absorbed the region into the province of Iudaea.
